name: Design a Video Conferencing Service
intent: Let people meet by live video and audio, from two people to thousands, over home and mobile networks of very different quality, with a delay low enough for conversation.
codeTitle: an SFU picking simulcast layers for each viewer
finalIntro: One person joining a meeting, and the media flowing through the server.
prompt: Design a Zoom or Google Meet style service. People join a meeting from a browser or an app, see and hear each other with a delay under about 300 ms, can share a screen, and the meeting can be recorded. Meetings range from two people to several thousand watching a few speakers, and users are spread over the world with networks that are fast, slow, or behind strict firewalls.
functional: Create, schedule and join a meeting with a link
Send and receive live audio and video, and share a screen
Show a grid of participants and highlight the person speaking
Mute, raise a hand, and chat during the meeting
Record a meeting and make the recording available afterwards
Support meetings from two people up to thousands of viewers
nonFunctional: Mouth-to-ear delay under about 300 ms, and audio must stay smooth even when video suffers
Join a meeting in a few seconds
Adapt to each participant's changing bandwidth without stopping the meeting
Work for people behind firewalls and NATs, including those that block UDP
Millions of concurrent participants, with the cost of media servers kept in check
Media is encrypted in transit, and only people who are allowed in can join

firstAttempt.text: Browsers connect directly to each other in a full mesh over WebRTC. Everyone sends a copy of their camera to every other participant, and each one decodes all the others. A small server only helps the browsers to find each other.
limits: Each participant uploads N-1 copies of their video, so with 8 people a home uplink of 10 Mbit/s is already full
Each participant also encodes N-1 times and decodes N-1 streams, which overloads a laptop or phone at around 5 to 6 people
Many pairs cannot connect directly because of NATs and firewalls, and nothing relays them
A single slow participant cannot be given a lower quality without hurting the sender's other connections
There is nowhere to record the meeting, and the number of connections grows with the square of the participants

steps.title: Set up calls with signaling, ICE, STUN and TURN
steps.problem: Two browsers behind home routers (which use NAT, so the browser only knows a private address) do not know each other's addresses, cannot accept incoming connections, and need to agree on codecs and keys before they can exchange a single frame.
steps.fix: Participants keep a WebSocket to a signaling server, which only carries small messages: who is in the meeting, session descriptions (SDP offers and answers describing codecs and encryption keys) and ICE candidates. Each side gathers candidate addresses: its own, the public address learned from a STUN server, and a relayed address on a TURN server. Both sides try the pairs, prefer a direct UDP path, and fall back to the TURN relay (over UDP, TCP or TLS on port 443) when a firewall blocks everything else. Media then flows over encrypted SRTP, and the signaling server is no longer on the path.
steps.tradeoff: Calls connect for almost everyone, including strict corporate networks. TURN relays carry real traffic, and roughly 10 to 15 percent of connections end up on one, so it must be sized and placed near users. Signaling is cheap, but its connections are long-lived and must be spread and survive reconnects.

steps.title: Put a selective forwarding unit in the middle
steps.problem: A mesh makes every participant upload N-1 copies and decode N-1 streams, so it breaks down after four or five people.
steps.fix: Every participant sends one stream to a media server, a selective forwarding unit (SFU), and the SFU copies the packets to the others. The SFU does not decode or re-encode the video, it only reads packet headers and forwards, so one machine handles thousands of streams. The uplink of each client is one stream whatever the meeting size, and the SFU is also the natural place to relay clients behind firewalls and to tap the media for recording.
steps.tradeoff: Upload falls from N-1 streams to one, and a modest server serves many meetings. The server's outgoing traffic grows with the square of the participants in a meeting, every viewer still decodes every stream it shows, and a media server is now in the path of every call, so it must be kept close to users and replaced when it fails.

steps.title: Use simulcast and estimate the bandwidth of every link
steps.problem: With one stream per sender, a viewer with a poor connection receives the same 720p stream as everyone else, so it loses packets and the picture freezes, and the SFU cannot lower the quality without re-encoding.
steps.fix: Each sender encodes its camera at several qualities at once, for example 180p, 360p and 720p (simulcast), or one scalable stream whose layers can be dropped (SVC). The sender uploads as many layers as its uplink allows. For every viewer, the server estimates the available downlink from packet arrival times and feedback (transport-wide congestion control), divides it over the tiles shown, and forwards the highest layer that fits each tile, switching at a keyframe (a frame that can be decoded on its own). A small tile or a thumbnail gets the low layer, and the speaker gets the high one. Audio is sent first and protected with extra redundancy.
steps.tradeoff: Every viewer gets the best picture its link can carry, and slow viewers no longer hurt anyone. Senders spend more CPU and about 40 percent more upload on the extra layers, and the bandwidth estimate must react in a second or so without oscillating.

steps.title: Place SFUs near users and cascade them
steps.problem: A meeting with people in Frankfurt, Tokyo and Sao Paulo cannot have a good delay if everyone talks to one server in one place, and one machine cannot hold a very large meeting.
steps.fix: A meeting router assigns each participant to a media server in the nearest region, and the servers of one meeting are linked to each other (cascading): each server sends one copy of each stream to the other servers over the provider's backbone, instead of every participant crossing the ocean. Within a region, a large meeting spreads over several SFUs in the same way. The router picks servers by load and keeps a meeting together while it is small. Participants join the server that is closest, using DNS or anycast and latency probes.
steps.tradeoff: Each participant has a short, stable first hop, the long distance is travelled once over a good private network, and a meeting can grow beyond one machine. There is a little extra delay for each server hop, more state to coordinate, and failures of a server or a link between servers must be repaired while the call continues.

steps.title: Record by joining the meeting as a hidden participant
steps.problem: People want a recording with all video, the shared screen and the audio in one file, but the media is encrypted, live and in many pieces on different servers.
steps.fix: The recorder joins the meeting like a participant, subscribes to the streams through the SFU, and writes them to storage. A first copy keeps the separate tracks (raw, cheap and flexible), and then a background job composes the tracks into one video and transcodes it into the formats people play. Audio and video tracks carry timestamps so that they can be lined up exactly, and the finished file is announced when it is ready. Consent is shown to all participants when recording starts.
steps.tradeoff: Live calls are not slowed by recording, because the heavy composing happens later, away from the media path. It needs storage and compute, the recording appears minutes after the meeting ends, and the separate tracks must be kept until the composed file is verified.

steps.title: Detect the dominant speaker and show only what matters
steps.problem: In a meeting of 200 people nobody can see 200 tiles, and a client cannot decode that many. Sending everything to everyone wastes the network and the CPU of every participant.
steps.fix: Each client reports the audio level of its microphone in an RTP header extension, so the SFU can read it without decoding the audio. The server smooths the levels over a few seconds and picks the dominant speaker, with some hysteresis so the highlight does not flip at every cough. Each viewer subscribes only to the last N active speakers plus the pinned or visible tiles (last-N), at the layer that fits the tile, and other participants appear as names. Very large webinars send a few presenters to thousands of viewers, who receive a single layered or HLS-like stream through the cascade.
steps.tradeoff: Client CPU and every network link are kept in check, however large the meeting is, and the conversation focuses on whoever is talking. The picture changes as people speak, a late subscription needs a keyframe request, and the detection thresholds need tuning so that noise and echo do not steal the highlight.

failures.scenario: A media server crashes during a meeting
failures.impact: Everyone connected to it loses audio and video at once.
failures.answer: Clients notice that packets stopped, ask the signaling server for a new server, and restart ICE with an ICE restart. The meeting router picks a healthy server, often the same region, and the cascade is re-linked. People are back within a few seconds. Meeting state such as the roster and who is muted lives outside the media server, so it survives.

failures.scenario: A participant's network drops to almost nothing
failures.impact: Their video freezes, and without care the whole meeting would wait for them.
failures.answer: Their own estimated bandwidth falls, so the SFU sends them only low layers and then stops video, keeping audio, which needs just 30 to 50 kbit/s. Their uplink is cut to the lowest layer or audio only. Other viewers do not slow down, because the SFU adapts per link, and full quality returns step by step when the network recovers.

failures.scenario: A company network blocks UDP and all unknown ports
failures.impact: Direct connections and UDP relays fail, and the person cannot join.
failures.answer: ICE falls back to a TURN server over TCP and then TLS on port 443, which looks like ordinary web traffic. The call works with a larger delay and more risk of freezes, because TCP retransmits old packets. The client reports it, so that dashboards show which networks are in this state.

failures.scenario: A famous speaker opens a webinar for 20,000 viewers
failures.impact: One SFU cannot send 20,000 copies of the stream, and all the viewers arrive within a minute.
failures.answer: The meeting router spreads the viewers over many SFUs that are cascaded from the one holding the presenter, each receiving a single copy. Viewers get a lower layer and see only the presenter, and joins are metered so that the signaling and the servers are not overwhelmed. Extra servers are started ahead of the scheduled start.

alternatives.title: How the media travels

options.name: Mesh
options.pro: No media servers to pay for, and the lowest delay for two people
options.con: Upload and CPU grow with the meeting, so it works only up to about 4 people

options.name: SFU
options.pro: Forwards without decoding, so it is cheap, and every participant sends one stream
options.con: The server's output grows with the square of the meeting, and clients decode every stream shown

options.name: MCU
options.pro: Each client sends and receives one stream, which suits weak devices and old room systems
options.con: The server decodes and encodes everything, which costs roughly ten to fifty times more CPU, and the layout is fixed

alternatives.pick: An SFU for nearly everything, mesh for two-person calls, and an MCU only as a gateway for devices that need a mixed stream.

alternatives.title: How to send several qualities

options.name: Simulcast
options.pro: Separate independent streams, supported everywhere, simple to switch
options.con: Upload is the sum of the layers, and each layer is encoded in full

options.name: SVC (scalable video coding)
options.pro: One stream with dropable layers, so less upload and cheaper switching
options.con: Needs codec support (VP9, AV1), and not every client has it

alternatives.pick: Simulcast by default, and SVC where both ends support it.

alternatives.title: Where to place media servers

options.name: One server per meeting, near the first participant
options.pro: Simple, and a small meeting needs one hop
options.con: Distant participants suffer a long delay

options.name: Nearest server for every participant, with cascading
options.pro: Short first hop for everyone, and the meeting can grow
options.con: More coordination and an extra hop between servers

alternatives.pick: Nearest region for each participant with cascading, and a single server for small local meetings.

alternatives.title: How recordings are made

options.name: Record at the client
options.con: Fails if the participant leaves or the browser crashes, and quality depends on their network

options.name: Server-side recorder as a participant
options.pro: Reliable, independent of anyone's device, and can be processed afterwards

alternatives.pick: A server-side recorder that saves tracks, then composes them in a background job.

roles.label: Participants
roles.description: Browsers and apps that capture, encode and show the media.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: Signaling, STUN and TURN, and the meeting router.

roles.label: Recording pipeline
roles.description: The recorder that works off the live path.

roles.label: Media processing
roles.description: SFUs, layer selection and speaker detection.

quiz.question: An 8-person call uses a full-mesh WebRTC design. Each participant sends a 2 Mbit/s camera stream to every other person. People on 10 Mbit/s home uplinks report frozen video and laptops running hot. The team wants the fix to keep server cost low. What should they do?
options: Send every connection through a TURN relay, so that the relay carries the load instead of the participants' uplinks
Upload one stream to a selective forwarding unit, which copies packets to the others without decoding them
Lower every camera to 360p in meetings above four people, so that seven copies fit within the uplink
Replace the mesh with an MCU that decodes all streams and mixes them into one picture for each participant
quiz.explanation: Seven copies of 2 Mbit/s is 14 Mbit/s, more than the uplink, and an SFU cuts that to one copy while only forwarding packets, which is cheap. A TURN relay still receives seven copies from each sender. Lowering to 360p fits the uplink, but every laptop still encodes and decodes seven streams and stays hot, and quality falls for everyone. An MCU also works, but decoding and encoding everything costs many times more server CPU.

quiz.question: In a 12-person meeting through an SFU, each sender uploads one 720p stream of 1.5 Mbit/s. A viewer on a 4 Mbit/s downlink is shown all 11 tiles and sees constant freezes, while everyone else is fine. What should the system do?
options: Have senders upload several qualities (simulcast), and forward each viewer the layer that fits its link
Make the SFU decode the 720p streams and re-encode a lower bitrate version for that one viewer
Ask all 12 senders to drop to 240p, so that the slowest viewer can keep up with every tile
Increase the viewer's jitter buffer to 2 seconds, so that late packets can be reassembled before playback
quiz.explanation: Eleven streams of 1.5 Mbit/s is 16.5 Mbit/s, far above 4, so the viewer needs lower layers for small tiles. Simulcast lets the SFU pick per viewer without decoding anything. Re-encoding defeats the point of an SFU, and lowering everyone hurts people with good links. A 2-second jitter buffer only adds delay, since it cannot create bandwidth the link lacks.

quiz.question: A webinar has one presenter and 20,000 viewers. The presenter's stream is 1 Mbit/s, and each SFU server has a 10 Gbit/s network link. Everyone joins within a minute. How should the media be delivered?
options: Put one SFU in front of all the viewers and let the presenter publish to it, on the biggest machine available
Add 20 SFU servers behind a load balancer, with the presenter's client publishing its stream to each of them
Use an MCU to mix the meeting into one composite stream, which removes the need for separate copies per viewer
Spread viewers over many SFUs that each receive one cascaded copy of the presenter's stream, at a lower layer
quiz.explanation: 20,000 copies of 1 Mbit/s is 20 Gbit/s, more than one server link can send. Cascading means the presenter uploads once and each edge SFU fans out to its own viewers. Publishing to 20 servers multiplies the presenter's uplink, and mixing into one stream still needs 20,000 outgoing copies.
